title: The Burden of Tyre
overview: Isaiah 23 pronounces a prophetic oracle against the ancient maritime city of Tyre, a powerful and wealthy trading hub known for its extensive commerce and influence. The chapter vividly describes the impending destruction and desolation of Tyre, portraying it as a divine judgment decreed by the LORD of hosts. It highlights Tyre’s pride and economic strength, the mourning of its trading partners, and the eventual restoration after a seventy-year period of desolation. This chapter serves as a sobering reminder of God's sovereignty over nations and commerce, illustrating that even the mightiest cities are subject to His judgment and purposes. It also anticipates a future restoration that aligns with God’s redemptive plan for the nations.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: The Lament for Tyre’s Destruction.** The chapter opens with a call for mourning from the ships of Tarshish and the inhabitants of the island, emphasizing the total devastation of Tyre and the impact on its trading partners.

**Verses 6-12: The Divine Judgment Announced.** This section reveals the divine counsel behind Tyre’s downfall, highlighting the LORD’s purpose to humble the proud city and destroy its strongholds, affecting even its closest allies.

**Verses 13-14: Historical Reflection and Mourning.** The prophecy recalls the rise and fall of the Chaldeans and calls again for the ships of Tarshish to lament Tyre’s loss of strength.

**Verses 15-18: The Seventy Years of Desolation and Future Restoration.** The chapter concludes with a prophecy of a seventy-year period during which Tyre will be forgotten, followed by a restoration where Tyre’s commerce will be consecrated to the LORD, symbolizing a renewed purpose under divine sovereignty.

keyVerses.text: The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals that Tyre’s destruction is not random but a deliberate act of God to humble human pride and worldly glory, underscoring God's supreme authority over all nations and their achievements.

keyVerses.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king: after the end of seventy years shall Tyre sing as an harlot.
keyVerses.significance: This prophecy sets a specific timeframe for Tyre’s desolation and foretells a future restoration, illustrating God’s sovereign control over history and the eventual renewal of even judged nations.

keyVerses.text: And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.
keyVerses.significance: This verse points to a transformed purpose for Tyre’s commerce, where its wealth is dedicated to God’s service, symbolizing redemption and the sanctification of material blessings for the people of God.

characters.name: Tyre
characters.description: A prominent Phoenician city-state renowned for its maritime trade and wealth. In this chapter, Tyre is the subject of divine judgment due to its pride and influence, representing worldly power that faces God’s sovereign correction.

characters.name: The LORD of Hosts
characters.description: God is the sovereign judge who decrees the destruction and eventual restoration of Tyre. His purpose is to humble human pride and demonstrate His authority over all nations and their commerce.

characters.name: Merchants of Zidon and Tarshish
characters.description: These represent Tyre’s trading partners and allies who mourn the city’s downfall. Their lamentation underscores the wide-reaching impact of Tyre’s judgment on international trade and alliances.

themes.description: The chapter emphasizes God’s supreme authority over nations and their fortunes, showing that even powerful cities like Tyre are subject to His will and judgment.
Tyre’s pride and self-exaltation provoke divine judgment, reflecting the biblical principle that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.
The prophecy illustrates how God can bring down economic and political powers, reminding believers that material wealth and influence are temporary and subordinate to God’s plan.
Despite judgment, God promises restoration after a period of desolation, symbolizing hope and the possibility of renewal under God’s blessing.

historicalContext: Tyre was a major Phoenician city located on the Mediterranean coast, flourishing around the 8th century BC as a center of maritime trade and commerce. Its strategic position and naval power made it influential across the ancient Near East and Mediterranean regions. The reference to Tarshish and Zidon highlights Tyre’s extensive trade networks. The seventy-year period mentioned likely corresponds to a time of Babylonian dominance and destruction of cities allied with or similar to Tyre. The Assyrian and Babylonian empires were the dominant political forces during this era, often clashing with Phoenician city-states. Understanding this geopolitical context helps clarify the prophecy’s significance as a divine judgment against a proud and powerful commercial empire.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This interpretation emphasizes God’s sovereign control over history and nations, viewing Tyre’s judgment as a demonstration of God’s justice against pride and idolatry, with the restoration pointing to God’s redemptive mercy.

Dispensationalists see the seventy years as a literal period of judgment, often linked to Babylonian captivity, with Tyre’s restoration foreshadowing future millennial blessings and the inclusion of Gentile nations in God’s kingdom.

Early church interpreters often saw Tyre as a symbol of worldly corruption and materialism, with its fall representing the ultimate defeat of earthly powers opposed to God’s kingdom and the hope of spiritual renewal.

crossReferences.connection: This passage also prophesies the destruction of Tyre, providing a parallel account of its judgment and emphasizing God’s sovereignty over the city.
Tyre is symbolically referenced as a representation of a great commercial city destined for judgment, linking Isaiah’s prophecy to end-times themes.
Mentions Tyre among the nations subject to Babylonian judgment, reinforcing the historical context of Tyre’s downfall.
God’s sovereign laughter at the nations’ plots echoes the theme of divine control over earthly powers seen in Isaiah 23.
God’s decree over kingdoms and rulers aligns with the divine purpose behind Tyre’s judgment.

application: Trust in God's sovereignty over all nations and circumstances, recognizing that no human power is beyond His control.
Avoid pride and self-exaltation, remembering that God resists the proud and humbles the mighty.
Recognize that material wealth and success are temporary and should be used for God’s glory.
Find hope in God’s promise of restoration even after seasons of judgment or hardship.
Pray for wisdom to steward resources in ways that honor God and serve His purposes.
Encourage faithfulness in difficult times, trusting that God’s plans ultimately bring redemption.
conclusion: Isaiah 23 stands as a powerful testament to God’s sovereign authority over the proud and prosperous city of Tyre, illustrating the certainty of divine judgment against human arrogance and the fleeting nature of worldly power. Yet, it also offers hope through the promise of restoration, reminding believers that God’s purposes include redemption and renewal. This chapter challenges Christians to submit to God’s rule, reject pride, and trust in His timing for restoration, applying these truths to their own lives and communities.
timeline: c. 740-700 BC - Prophetic ministry of Isaiah during the rise of Assyrian and Babylonian empires
